tagline.text: Ilocos Norte's largest freshwater lake, with a mansion museum and a water park on its shore

location.label: Location
location.text: Around Barangay Suba, north of Paoay, Ilocos Norte, bordering Laoag City

budget.label: Budget

children.text: Paoay Lake covers about 3.86 km², making it the largest lake in Ilocos Norte, and lies behind sand dunes about 3 km inland from the sea. In half a day you can combine the Malacañang of the North mansion museum on the high ground by the shore, a floating water playground and a lakeside sunset.

Paoay Lake is the largest lake in Ilocos Norte, north of the town of Paoay. In the local Ilocano language it is called Dakél a Danum, meaning "big water," and old records also call it Lago de Nanguyudan. According to Wikipedia its area is about 3.86 km² (386 hectares; PhilAtlas lists about 328 hectares, so sources vary between roughly 3.3 and 3.9 km²), its average depth is about 6 m, its deepest point is reported to be about 10 m, and it lies about 3 km from the sea. No major river flows into it; it is a freshwater lake filled by groundwater and rainwater running off the surrounding hills in the rainy season. It sits between the coastal dunes to the northwest and the sea, so on a clear day low hills curve around the far side of the lake.

The lake has a legend, too. It tells of a prosperous village called San Juan de Sahagún that sank in an earthquake and became the lake. Scientifically, it is explained as water trapped behind a sand barrier that formed as the coast grew seaward in the late Quaternary. Its protection history is long: in 1969 Republic Act 5631 made the lake and about 1 km around it a national park; in 1978 Presidential Decree 1554 reduced the park to the lake proper at its highest water level (to respect existing occupants' land claims); and in 2025 Republic Act 12230 made it the Paoay Lake Protected Landscape (set by the law at about 347 hectares). As a result, development along the shore is limited and the surroundings remain relatively calm.

For travelers, the attractions gathered on the shore matter more than the lake itself. On a hill by the lake, Malacañang of the North (Malacañang ti Amianan in Ilocano), built in 1977, looks down over the water. It operates as a museum with an admission fee and, along with the lake, is the most visited sight here. There is an 18-hole Paoay golf course, and lodging nearby includes Fort Ilocandia Resort and Plaza del Norte Hotel. The Paoay Lake Waterpark, which floats inflatable slides and an obstacle course on the lake, adds to the appeal for families.

The lake is tied to local livelihoods as well. Tilapia fish pens line its edge, and tilapia, catfish and mudfish live in the water along with aquatic plants. Resident birds such as the white-collared kingfisher, brahminy kite and Philippine duck, and migratory birds such as the grey heron, osprey and great egret, are said to be seen over the lake. The slanting light at sunrise and sunset is the most beautiful, and since midday sun is strong with little shade, early morning or late afternoon is more comfortable. This guide draws on Wikipedia, Ilocos Norte's official tourism information and recent travel articles; fees and hours can change, so confirm them locally.

From the road that runs along the lake you can watch the sunset blend water and sky into one color. Which sections of the shore are accessible differs from place to place, so check locally and watch for traffic along the road edge. Mosquitoes increase at dusk, so bring repellent.

This two-story bahay na bato–style mansion, built in 1977, stands on a hill overlooking the lake. It has seven rooms, each themed on study, agriculture, diplomacy, overseas workers, culture, nation building or family. According to the official tourism information, admission is

blocks.title: Paoay golf course and lakeside resorts

children.text: There is an 18-hole golf course on the shore, and Fort Ilocandia Resort and Plaza del Norte Hotel are nearby. Even if you are not there to play golf, you can enjoy the lake view from the hotel restaurants and gardens. Ask directly about the conditions for using the facilities.

blocks.title: Tilapia fish pens and lake people

children.text: Small fish pens on the shore are where local residents raise tilapia. These are private facilities, so ask permission before going close.

Resident and migratory birds such as the white-collared kingfisher, brahminy kite and Philippine duck can be seen over the lake. They are easiest to find early in the morning with binoculars. Please do not chase the birds or feed them.

Paoay Church, close to the lake, is a UNESCO World Heritage earthquake Baroque church. A common plan is to visit the church in the morning and the lake in the afternoon as one route. For the church itself, see the Paoay Church entry.
Sand dunes stretch along the coast near the lake, where you can try a 4×4 ride and sandboarding. The official tourism information lists a 1-hour 4×4 ride at
(for 5 people). It can be combined with the lake on the same day, but it is very hot at midday in summer.

items.title: From Manila by air and road

children.text: There are direct flights from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Laoag International Airport. Airlines and times vary by season, so check when you book.
From the airport, the route to the lake is described as following the Laoag–Balaccad Road. You can use a taxi, a tricycle or a booked car.
You can also go from Manila to Laoag by overnight bus, which takes about
9–11 hours
Take a jeepney bound for Paoay town from the Laoag jeepney terminal. It takes about
30–40 minutes
From town to the lake is about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle. If you are traveling alone, a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) is cheaper.
For a group, renting a vehicle or hiring a driver in Laoag is more convenient.
Facilities along the shore are often some distance apart, so chartering a tricycle is easier than walking. The fare is negotiated, so settle it including waiting time.
The lake connects to the main highway by Paoay Lake Road.

Ilocos Norte has distinct dry and rainy seasons. From November to May there are many clear days, which is good for the lake sunset and outdoor activities. March to May is very hot, though, and with little shade at midday on the shore you tire easily unless you are in the water.

June to October is the rainy season, with frequent rain and typhoons. The lake level rises and the scenery turns green, but water facilities and dune rides sometimes stop because of the weather. Leave some slack in your plans and check the forecast.

For lodging you can choose places on the lakeshore such as Fort Ilocandia Resort and Plaza del Norte Hotel, or stay in Laoag city. The lakeside lodgings have good views and are linked with golf, while Laoag city has more restaurants and easier transport. Book early for holidays.
You can try Ilocos foods such as bagnet (fried pork) and empanada at lakeside restaurants and the town market. Menus vary by restaurant, so check prices first.

There are not many restaurants right by the lake, so it can be hard to find a seat at lunchtime. It is easier to eat first near the town market or bring water and snacks. After sunset it can be hard to find transport, so arrange your ride back in advance.
Plan the church and museum in the morning and the lake and sunset in the late afternoon to get less sun.
The water park requires life vests and has height and age limits, so check in advance if you bring children.
Lakeside restaurants and facilities get crowded around sunset. On holidays, grab your seat early.
If you charter a tricycle, agree on the round-trip fare including waiting time beforehand.
Get into the lake water only inside facilities, and stay away from the fish pens and nets.
Dress modestly for the Malacañang museum and the church, and operations differ by day of the week. Check the latest notices.
Bring insect repellent, a hat and sunscreen.
Keep a light raincoat in your bag for rainy days, and wear shoes that can get wet on the shore.
The lake is a protected landscape, so protect its water quality and wildlife habitat. Do not litter or catch fish or birds.
Water facilities may close depending on lake conditions and weather.
There is little shade at midday and a risk of heatstroke, so drink water often.
Roads along the lake may have few streetlights after dark, so move before sunset.
Fees and hours change with the season. Check the official tourism information or each facility's notices just before you go.
Do not swim in the lake outside the facilities. Depth, aquatic plants and nets can make it dangerous.
